I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-04-09 09:40 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-04-09T08:40:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 43.368 degrees and its azimuth is 85.647 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 30.621 degrees and its azimuth is 232.237 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 58.18 percent illuminated, 99.256 degrees from the Sun, and 399264.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Yes—very likely.

The Moon is well above the horizon at **30.6° altitude**, in the **southwest** (azimuth **232°**, roughly southwest), and it is **58% illuminated**. Its angular separation from the Sun is about **99°**, so it is far enough from the Sun to be a readily observable daytime Moon. At a distance of about **399,000 km**, it is also near its normal apparent size.

The main challenge is the bright daylight sky, not the Moon’s position. From Lagos at that time, look toward the **southwest**, about one-third of the way from the horizon to overhead. If possible, use a location with a clear horizon and shade your eyes from direct sunlight—but **do not look near the Sun**, even briefly, through binoculars or a telescope.

Given the clear sky and your normal eyesight, you should be able to spot it with the naked eye, though it may take a minute or two of searching.
